records.title: 3.4L V6 Intake Manifold and Head Gasket Coolant Leaks (Dex-Cool)
records.description: The 3.4L LA1 V6 in every Aztek uses nylon-carrier lower intake manifold gaskets that degrade in long-life Dex-Cool coolant, causing internal and external coolant leaks; prolonged leakage leads to overheating, warped heads, and blown head gaskets. CarComplaints rates the 2001 blown head gasket problem 8.8/10 ('pretty bad') at an average $1,470 and 99,000 miles, and the 2003 intake gasket coolant leak averages $1,200 at just 57,000 miles. Coolant mixing with oil can destroy the engine if the leak is ignored, with some owners forced into full engine replacement.
records.solution: Replace the lower intake manifold gaskets with updated Fel-Pro 'Problem Solver' metal-carrier gaskets and perform a full cooling system flush. If the engine overheated, have the heads checked for warpage and replace head gaskets as needed. Service Dex-Cool on time and never let the system run low.
symptoms: Unexplained coolant loss with no visible puddle
Low coolant light or repeated topping-off
Engine overheating
Milky or chocolate-colored oil on the dipstick
Orange sludge in the coolant reservoir
White exhaust smoke

records.title: 4T65-E Transmission Failure and Pressure Control Solenoid Erratic Shifting
records.description: The Aztek's 4T65-E four-speed automatic suffers from pressure control (force motor) solenoid failure that drives line pressure to maximum, causing harsh shifting and accelerating internal wear; GM addressed related harsh-shift complaints in TSB 02-07-30-022B (faulty transaxle connectors, 2001-2004) and cold-weather reverse servo seal shrinkage in TSB 04-07-30-028. NHTSA complaints for the 2003 Aztek document gear failure, no-forward-movement, and shifter problems at an average of about 157,000 miles. Left unaddressed, the harsh-shift condition commonly progresses to slipping and loss of 3rd/4th gear requiring a rebuild or replacement.
records.solution: Diagnose stored codes first: P1811 with harsh shifts points to the pressure control solenoid, which requires removing the transmission side cover (engine cradle lowered) to replace. Severely slipping or non-driving units need a rebuilt or remanufactured 4T65-E. Fluid and filter service every 50,000 miles extends solenoid and clutch life.

records.title: Erratic Fuel Gauge from Failed Fuel Level Sensor
records.description: The in-tank fuel level sender on the Aztek wears and corrodes, making the fuel gauge bounce between full and empty (typically once the tank drops below half), read full constantly, or falsely trigger the low-fuel light. NHTSA and owner complaints document failures clustering around 50,000 miles, and corrosion in the sender connector or wiring produces the same erratic behavior. Owners cannot trust the gauge and risk running out of fuel without warning.
records.solution: Replace the fuel level sensor/sending unit, which on the Aztek requires dropping the fuel tank to access the pump module — many shops recommend replacing the complete pump module at the same time given the labor overlap. Inspect and clean the sender connector and wiring for corrosion before condemning the sender.

records.title: Instrument Cluster Stepper Motor Failure — Stuck, Pegged, or Erratic Gauges
records.description: The Aztek's instrument cluster uses factory gauge stepper motors with an internal material/design flaw that causes short service life — once one fails, the rest typically follow. Owners see speedometer, tach, fuel, and temperature needles stick, peg past maximum, or read erratically, along with dim or dead backlighting and blank odometer/PRND displays from cracked solder joints. Multiple dedicated repair services exist solely for the 2001-2005 Aztek cluster, reflecting how widespread the failure is across GM vehicles of this era.
records.solution: Repair rather than replace: install updated Switec X27.168 stepper motors (the GM-authorized replacement), renew the backlight bulbs, and reflow the cracked solder joints. Mail-in cluster rebuild services do all of this with a warranty; handy DIYers can replace the motors with a soldering iron for under $100 in parts.
symptoms: Speedometer needle stuck, pegged, or jumping erratically
Fuel, tach, or temperature gauges reading wrong or dead
Dash backlighting dim or out
Blank odometer or PRND display
Entire cluster intermittently going dead

records.title: Aztek/Rendezvous Intermediate Steering Shaft — 2003 Recall + General Clunk Issue
records.description: 2001-2005 Aztek and 2002-2005 Buick Rendezvous (GMT257 platform) have two related intermediate-steering-shaft issues. (1) NHTSA recall for certain 2003-model Aztek and Rendezvous (Product Field Action Bulletin 03009) — an undersize intermediate shaft can spin inside the steering-column coupling, causing total loss of directional control with no prior warning. (2) Across all years: the intermediate-shaft splines dry out and develop a pronounced clunk when turning the wheel or going over bumps. Not a safety issue once recall remedy is in place, but very noticeable.
records.solution: Recall: check VIN at NHTSA — affected 2003 cars get free shaft replacement. General clunk: disassemble the intermediate shaft, clean and re-lube splines with synthetic grease (DIY) or pay ~$80 shop labor. If splines are visibly worn, replace the shaft ($150-$300 part). GM "shaft lube kit" with snap-in collar is a durable fix.

records.title: Premature Front Wheel Hub Bearing Failure
records.description: Front hub/bearing assemblies on the Aztek wear out far earlier than normal — NHTSA complaints on the 2002 model alone document 14 failures from as low as 8,700 miles, with owners reporting the same hub replaced up to five times and a technician calling it 'a common problem with all Azteks.' Because the wheel speed sensor is built into the hub, a failing bearing also corrupts the ABS signal, triggering ABS/traction warnings and disabling the Versatrak AWD system on equipped models. Ignored long enough, a collapsed bearing causes wheel wobble and a genuine safety hazard.
records.solution: Replace the failed hub/bearing assembly with a quality (preferably OE-grade) unit, torque the axle nut to spec, and clean the integrated wheel speed sensor connector to clear ABS/AWD warnings. Inspect both sides — owners frequently report sequential failure of the opposite hub.

Noise changes when steering left or right
ABS or traction control light on

Wobble or looseness felt in the steering

records.title: Rear Liftgate Electronic Release Failure — Hatch Will Not Open
records.description: The Aztek's rear hatch has no mechanical handle — even the key cylinder works through an electronic release — so when the latch actuator, its wiring, or the release circuit fails, the hatch cannot be opened at all from the fob, the button, or the key. CarComplaints logs this as a distinct problem on 2001 and 2002 models, and owners report intermittent operation, the gate hanging on its secondary latch, and only temporary fixes from battery disconnects or fuse swaps. Worn gas struts compound the problem by letting an opened hatch slam back down.
records.solution: Replace the failed liftgate latch/release actuator (accessed by removing the interior hatch trim and manually tripping the latch with a screwdriver while an assistant pulls the gate). Check the release circuit fuse and wiring first, and replace both gas struts if the hatch will not stay up.

records.title: Versatrak AWD Rear Differential Failure — AWD Disable Light and Clutch Chatter
records.description: AWD Azteks use GM's Versatrak system with a rear differential containing twin gerotor-pump-driven clutch packs that run a special vegetable-based fluid which breaks down quickly; degraded fluid causes clutch chatter and groaning in tight turns, and clutch pump check-valve failures trigger the 'AWD Disable' warning and shut the system down. High-mileage units also develop pinion and axle seal leaks that, if unnoticed, starve the unit and destroy the clutches and bearings. The vehicle keeps driving as front-wheel drive, but restoring AWD often means rebuilding or replacing the rear carrier.
records.solution: Change the Versatrak rear differential fluid with the correct GM fluid every 15,000-30,000 miles — early fluid service cures most chatter and groaning. Fix seal leaks promptly; once the clutch pumps or check valves fail, the accepted repair is a rebuilt or good used rear carrier assembly (GM part 88894200 era).

Groaning, shuddering, or chatter from the rear during slow tight turns

records.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor / Ignition Control Module Failure Causing Stalling and No-Start
records.description: Failing crankshaft position sensors and ignition control modules are among the most common causes of intermittent stalling and no-spark no-start conditions on 3800-powered Bonnevilles, documented by RepairPal as a known model problem. The CKP sensor's hall-effect elements degrade with heat, causing the engine to randomly die while driving — often with no trouble code — and frequently restart only after cooling down. The ICM, which needs both 18X and 3X/sync crank signals to fire the coils, exhibits the same heat-related intermittent failure.
records.solution: Test the crank sensor and ICM circuits and replace the failed component; the dual CKP sensor sits behind the harmonic balancer, so the crank pulley must be pulled, and a crank relearn may be required after replacement. Many high-mileage owners replace the CKP sensor and ICM together to end repeat intermittent stalls.
symptoms: Engine stalls randomly while driving
Restarts only after sitting and cooling down
Cranks but no start with no spark
Tachometer drops to zero before a stall
Check engine light may or may not illuminate

records.title: Fuel Tank Pressure Sensor Defect — Fuel Leak and Fire Risk (NHTSA Recall 03V238000, SSEi)
records.description: NHTSA campaign 03V238000/GM 03038 covers certain 2002-2003 Pontiac Bonneville SSEi vehicles equipped with the supercharged 3.8L V6. The fuel-tank pressure sensor may malfunction and allow excessive vacuum during self-diagnostic testing; resulting fuel-system damage can permit a leak during refueling and create a fire risk in the presence of an ignition source. NHTSA lists 102,212 total vehicles across the multi-make campaign, not 102,212 Bonnevilles. The campaign record does not establish the frozen page's added inaccurate-gauge, tank-noise, poor-driveability or P0452/P0453 symptom set.
records.solution: Check the VIN in the NHTSA and GM recall systems for campaign 03V238000/03038 completion or an open remedy. If fuel odor or leakage is present, stop refueling, shut the vehicle off away from ignition sources, do not restart it, and arrange qualified inspection. The campaign remedy is dealer replacement of the fuel-tank pressure sensor; current availability and any charge for a vehicle of this age must be confirmed with GM rather than promised here. Do not buy a pressure sensor or other EVAP/fuel-system part from this page; recall eligibility, leak condition, part number and VIN fitment must be established first.

records.title: Mass Air Flow (MAF) Sensor Contamination and Failure
records.description: The MAF sensor on OBD-II 3800-powered Bonnevilles is a frequent failure point: its hot-wire element becomes contaminated with dirt or oil (often from over-oiled aftermarket filters) or the sensor electronics fail outright, sending a low or erratic frequency signal to the PCM and setting codes P0101/P0102. The result is hesitation, stumbling, rough idle, lack of power, and stalling. A classic 3800 diagnostic trick — the engine running noticeably better with the MAF unplugged — confirms the sensor as the culprit.
records.solution: Clean the sensor element with dedicated MAF cleaner as a first step; if symptoms or codes return, replace the MAF sensor, a common and straightforward repair on these cars. Also verify the intake tube is sealed and check the MAF/O2 fuse, which feeds the sensor's 12V supply.

Stalling at idle or when coming to a stop
Check engine light with P0101/P0102

records.title: Plastic Upper Intake Manifold (Plenum) Degradation and Coolant Ingestion (3800 Series II)
records.description: The composite plastic upper intake manifold on the 3800 Series II V6 degrades over time, most notoriously around the hot EGR stovepipe passage, allowing coolant to leak internally into the intake runners or externally near the throttle body/thermostat area. Left unaddressed, coolant pooling in the intake can be drawn into the cylinders and hydrolock the engine, bending rods or destroying it outright.
records.solution: Replace the upper intake manifold with an updated unit (aftermarket versions include a reinforced/aluminum EGR sleeve) along with new gaskets; most shops replace the lower intake gaskets at the same time since access overlaps. Monitor coolant level closely and never keep driving an engine that is consuming coolant with no visible leak.

White sweet-smelling exhaust smoke at startup
Rough idle or misfire, especially after sitting
Low coolant warning light

records.title: SSEi Supercharger Nose-Drive Coupler and Bearing Wear (Eaton M62/M90)
records.description: The Eaton roots-type supercharger on the Bonneville SSEi (M62 on 1992-1995 Series I, M90 on 1996-2003 Series II) uses a plastic isolator coupler and snout bearings that wear out with age and mileage, typically past 100,000-120,000 miles. records.title: 700-R4/4L60E Automatic Transmission 3-4 Clutch Pack Failure
records.description: The TH700-R4 (third gen) and its electronic successor the 4L60E (fourth gen) are widely known for burning up the 3-4 clutch pack, especially behind the torquey LT1 and LS1 V8s. records.solution: A quality rebuild that addresses the root cause — Sonnax/TransGo corrective parts, upgraded 3-4 clutch pack and band, and verification of proper line-pressure rise — is the accepted fix. A parts-swap rebuild without these corrections commonly fails again within tens of thousands of miles.

records.title: Firebird LT1 Optispark Distributor Failure
records.description: 1993-1997 Firebird/Trans Am with the LT1 5.7L V8 (same engine in Camaro Z28, Corvette C4, and some Buick Roadmaster/Caprice/Impala SS) suffers infamous Optispark distributor failure. The distributor sits at the front of the engine behind the water pump — coolant leaks from the water pump (or condensation from the front of the engine) drip directly into the Optispark and short the optical sensors. records.title: Pop-Up Headlight Motor Gear Stripping (Headlights Stuck Up or Down)

records.title: Passlock Anti-Theft System False Activation Causing No-Start
records.description: The Passlock theft-deterrent sensor built into the ignition lock cylinder wears and sends an unstable resistance signal to the body control module, which then interprets a legitimate key as a theft attempt. The system disables the fuel injectors, leaving the car cranking but not starting with the SECURITY light flashing, and the failure typically recurs and worsens until owners are stranded repeatedly. This is one of the most widely documented complaints on the 1999-2005 Grand Am, with a 23+ page Edmunds thread and a RepairPal-confirmed pattern failure.

records.title: Front Strut-to-Tire Rub Destroying Inner Front Tire Sidewalls
records.description: The 2004-2006 GTO left the factory with marginal clearance between the front strut spring perch and the inner sidewall of the 245-width front tires. records.title: Blower Motor / HVAC Blower Resistor Failure
records.description: The Montana's heater/AC blower commonly fails due to a bad blower motor resistor or the blower motor itself. A classic symptom is the fan working only on the highest setting (which bypasses the resistor) while lower speeds are dead; in other cases the blower quits entirely or, less often, runs full-speed and won't shut off. Corrosion at the resistor connector is a frequent contributor.
records.solution: If only high speed works, replace the blower motor resistor (located near the blower motor, usually accessible behind dash trim). Test for power at the blower connector: power present but no fan means a bad motor; no power means a bad resistor (or relay/connector). Inspect and clean corroded connectors and check the relay and ground. Both repairs are inexpensive and require no programming.
symptoms: Blower only works on highest speed
No air from vents / blower dead
Inconsistent fan speeds
Blower runs constantly and won't shut off (resistor/relay)

records.title: Fuel Pump / Fuel System Failure Causing Stalling and No-Start
records.description: Montanas frequently develop fuel-delivery problems: in-tank fuel pump failure and clogged fuel filters cause hard starting, long crank times, intermittent stalling, and no-start conditions. A common pattern is the engine stalling when hot and restarting only after it cools, due to low fuel pressure. Corrosion at the fuel-tank-to-body wiring harness can also trigger a Check Engine Light or crank/no-start.
records.solution: Test fuel pressure to confirm; replace the in-tank fuel pump module if pressure is low and replace the fuel filter (recommended every ~30,000 miles to prevent overstressing the pump). Inspect and repair any corroded fuel-tank harness connectors. Rule out the fuel pump relay and crankshaft position sensor for intermittent stalling.

records.title: Instrument Cluster / Speedometer Stepper Motor Failure
records.description: Like many GM vehicles of this era, the Montana's instrument cluster suffers from failing Switec/Juken stepper motors and bad solder joints. Gauges — most often the speedometer, but also tach, fuel, and temperature — read erratically, stick, peg, or stop moving entirely. The odometer/gear-position digital display can also dim, flicker, or go dark. This is a widely documented design weakness, though no GM recall covers it.
records.solution: Send the cluster to a specialist (or DIY) to replace all gauge stepper motors with new Switec 27x.168 units and re-flow the solder joints. Because mileage is stored in the cluster, repair the existing unit rather than swapping in a used cluster from another vehicle, which would import the donor's mileage.

records.title: Convertible top water leaks into trunk and around rear window
records.description: The folding soft top is finicky and a frequent source of leaks. Water enters the trunk through the holes in the rear deck that accept the top's buttress pins (the seals don't fully seal) and through a slit in the trunk-lid hose that hides the top's flip cable. Owners also report wind noise and water at the back window when the top's drive-link socket falls out of adjustment, making the top hard to raise or stow.
records.solution: Reseal or replace the buttress-pin grommets and the trunk-lid cable hose, and clear/route the top's drainage. If the top won't stow or seal, readjust or reconnect the drive-link socket on the convertible top arm. Keep the trunk weatherstrip and rear deck seals in good condition.

records.title: Rear differential/driveline clunk and gear whine
records.description: Early Solstices are widely reported to develop a driveline clunk on take-up and shifting at low speed, plus a gear whine from the rear differential that changes with throttle. records.solution: GM issued TSBs covering the noise; the common fix for chatter-on-turns is a differential fluid drain and refill with the correct limited-slip additive (owners frequently use Royal Purple or a synthetic with friction modifier). Later cars received the driveline alignment redesign.

records.title: 4L60E automatic transmission 3-4 clutch pack failure
records.description: The 4L60E automatic (and its 700R4 predecessor) used across the 1990s Trans Am/Firebird is well known for burning up the 3-4 clutch pack. The 3-4 clutches see the highest load and heat, and failure is described by the F-body community and transmission specialists (Sonnax) as the number-one cause of a 4L60E dying. Contributing factors include GM's load-release springs in the clutch pack, a checkball/exhaust issue, a flex-prone OE backing plate, and line-pressure control affected by sensor faults. Once the 3-4 clutches burn, the transmission slips or loses 3rd and 4th gear entirely. High-mileage and hard-driven/modified cars are most affected.
records.solution: Rebuild the transmission with an upgraded 3-4 clutch pack (Raybestos GPZ or Borg-Warner Hi-Energy frictions are the community favorites), remove the problematic load-release springs, add a shift/valve-body correction kit and a stronger backing plate, and use fresh fluid and filter. Keeping the trans cool with an auxiliary cooler and servicing fluid on schedule extends life.

records.title: Early LS1 piston slap and high oil consumption
records.description: The 1998-1999 Trans Am/Firebird WS6 introduced the aluminum-block LS1 5.7L V8. Early LS1 engines are known for cold-start piston slap, a metallic knock or rattle at startup that quiets once the engine warms up. The root cause is the cast-iron cylinder sleeves not expanding as much as the surrounding aluminum, so cold pistons fit loosely in the bore. A related GM TSB (#01-06-01-023, covering 1999-2001 5.7L LS1 Camaro/Firebird/Corvette) documents higher-than-expected oil consumption (roughly 400-600 miles per quart) caused by a piston-ring-to-cylinder-bore interaction, especially in cars driven hard at high RPM. Not every engine is affected, and piston slap alone is generally not harmful, but the combination worried many owners.
records.solution: Cold-start piston slap that quiets when warm is generally considered cosmetic and can be monitored rather than repaired. For genuine excessive oil consumption, GM released updated higher-tension oil rings and a Napier second compression ring; severe cases require a ring job or short-block replacement. Regular oil-level checks and using the correct oil weight are the practical mitigations.
symptoms: Metallic knock/rattle at cold startup that quiets when warm
High oil consumption (approx 400-600 miles per quart)

records.title: LT1 Optispark distributor failure from moisture and ozone contamination
records.description: The 1993-1997 LT1-powered Trans Am/Firebird uses the Optispark (OptiSpark) optical ignition distributor mounted low on the front of the engine, behind the water pump and harmonic balancer. The optical cam-position sensor and high-voltage cap are extremely sensitive to moisture, and the confined location traps heat and ozone. Over time the ozone corrodes the cap contacts and any water intrusion (from the water pump weep hole, engine-bay washing, or condensation) shorts the optical sensor, causing failure. Early non-vented units are the worst; a later vented design (with two vacuum ports) improved things but did not eliminate the problem. This is one of the single most-discussed LT1 reliability items in the F-body community.
records.solution: Replace the Optispark with a vented-style unit (AC Delco or a quality aftermarket), replace the water pump at the same time since it must come off for access, and route a small hose from the water pump weep hole to divert coolant away from the distributor. Keep the engine bay dry and avoid pressure-washing near the front of the engine. Replacing plug wires while it is apart is standard practice.

Rough idle and misfire
Stumbling and hesitation on acceleration
Backfiring and sputtering
Black smoke from exhaust

records.title: LT1 water pump failure (shaft bearing/seal) with weep-hole coolant leak onto Optispark
records.description: The gear-driven LT1 water pump is a known wear item on 1993-1997 Trans Am/Firebird. Because the pump is mounted directly in front of the Optispark distributor, the weep hole is aimed toward the distributor and serpentine belt, so a leaking pump sprays coolant onto the ignition unit and accelerates Optispark failure. records.title: Pop-up headlight motor nylon gear stripping (4th-gen)
records.description: The 1993-1999 (4th-generation) Firebird/Trans Am uses electric pop-up headlight motors with an internal nylon drive gear. The plastic gear strips its teeth over time, so the motor spins but the headlight fails to raise or lower, or the light finishes moving and the motor keeps grinding for several seconds. records.title: T-top and roof weatherstrip leaks
records.description: T-top-equipped Trans Am/Firebirds (both 3rd-gen 1990-1992 and 4th-gen 1993-1999) commonly develop water leaks as the rubber seals age. The most frequent source is the U-shaped molding/weatherstrip around the top rear corner of the glass, which flattens and loses its shape after years of sun exposure and no longer seals against the glass, producing the classic wet-shoulder leak in heavy rain. records.title: EVAP System Faults — Charcoal Canister and Vent VSV Failure (P0440/P0441/P0446)
records.description: The Toyota-designed EVAP system used across the Vibe range is prone to the vacuum switching valve (VSV) on the charcoal canister sticking from dirt and weather exposure, and to the canister itself failing or becoming saturated, often after repeated fuel-tank topping-off. The result is the persistent check-engine-light trio P0440/P0441/P0446 (sometimes P0442), refueling problems where the pump nozzle clicks off repeatedly, and an automatic emissions-test failure in inspection states. This is one of the most common ownership complaints across GenVibe and Toyota Corolla/Matrix communities.
records.solution: First rule out a loose or worn gas cap, then test the vent VSV and replace it if stuck (a much cheaper repair than the full canister); replace the charcoal canister assembly if it is saturated or its integrated valves have failed. Stop topping off the tank after the nozzle clicks to avoid saturating the new canister.
symptoms: Check engine light with EVAP codes that return after clearing
Fuel nozzle clicks off repeatedly when refueling
Fuel smell near the rear of the car
Rough idle or hard start right after filling up
Failed state emissions inspection

records.title: Front Door Glass Bolts Loosen — Window Binds and Shatters (Recall 08V-162)
records.description: NHTSA campaign 08V-162 exactly covers 2003-2004 Pontiac Vibe vehicles equipped with power windows. Driver or front-passenger door-glass bolts may loosen, allowing the glass to separate from the regulator; abnormal noise can precede binding or shattering, creating distraction or injury risk. The indexed title, years and mechanism match the campaign. The total recall population spans Corolla, Matrix and Vibe and should not be presented as a Vibe-only complaint count.
records.solution: If a front window rattles, binds or shifts in the channel, stop operating it and keep hands clear of the glass. Check the VIN under campaign 08V-162/GM 07273 and contact an authorized GM dealer to confirm whether it is open and the current bolt inspection/replacement availability and charge. If glass has separated or shattered, secure the opening and use a qualified repairer. Do not buy bolts, a regulator or glass from this page; power-window equipment, affected side, damage, part number and VIN fitment must be established first.
symptoms: front power-window equipment confirmed
abnormal door noise or glass movement recorded
binding or separation checked without operating loose glass
VIN campaign status verified

records.title: Power Window Master Switch Overheats and Melts — Fire Risk (Recalls 12V-491 / 15V-689)
records.description: NHTSA campaign 12V-491 covers 2009 Vibe master switches produced with an imprecise lubrication process, and 15V-689 covers 2009-2010 Vibe switches with inconsistently applied grease. Unprotected sliding contacts may admit debris or moisture, short, overheat and melt, increasing fire risk. Together the campaigns support the frozen years and title; 12V-491 alone does not cover the 2010 Vibe.
records.solution: If the switch is hot, smells burned, smokes or shows melting, stop using it, turn the vehicle off when safe, move occupants away and call emergency services if fire is present. Check the VIN under 12V-491 and 15V-689 and contact an authorized GM dealer to confirm open status and current inspection/lubrication or circuit-board replacement availability and charge. Do not apply household or unapproved lubricant. Do not buy a switch from this page; campaign status, heat damage, part number and VIN fitment must be established first.
symptoms: switch sticking or abnormal feel recorded
heat, odor, smoke or melting checked without continued operation
VIN status checked against both campaigns
fire response used if smoke or flame is present

records.title: Takata Airbag Inflator Rupture — Including 2024 Do-Not-Drive Advisory (2003-2004)
records.description: Multiple NHTSA campaigns establish passenger-inflator rupture risk for Vibe vehicles, including 15V-285/15V-286 and 18V-883 for earlier cars and 16V-340, 17V-006, 18V-024 and 18V-025 for 2009-2010 zone populations. Degraded propellant can rupture the inflator and send metal fragments into occupants, causing serious injury or death. NHTSA and GM currently list certain 2003-2004 Pontiac Vibes with unrepaired Takata recalls under a Do Not Drive warning; this is VIN-specific, not every car in those model years. Campaign 20V-039 is a distinct replacement-airbag deployment issue and must not be described as the original rupture campaign.
records.solution: Check the VIN immediately in the NHTSA and GM recall lookups. If a 2003-2004 Vibe has an open Takata recall covered by the Do Not Drive warning, do not drive it; contact GM to arrange the current authorized remedy and ask about mobile repair or towing. For any open 2009-2010 inflator campaign, schedule the authorized remedy promptly. Confirm current availability and charge when scheduling. Do not buy or handle an inflator or airbag module from this page; campaign, VIN and repair history determine the remedy.
symptoms: VIN checked against current Takata campaigns
2003-2004 Do Not Drive status treated as VIN-specific
prior inflator or module replacement history reviewed
authorized remedy arranged without DIY airbag handling
affectedSystems: airbag module and prior replacement history

records.title: Unintended Acceleration — Sticking Accelerator Pedal and Floor Mat Entrapment (Recall 10V-024)
records.description: The 2009-2010 Vibe shares the Toyota Matrix's CTS accelerator pedal assembly and was swept into the Toyota unintended-acceleration recalls of January 2010, covering roughly 99,000 Vibes. The pedal's friction lever sliding surface can wear smooth and, with condensation, become slow to return or mechanically stick partially depressed; separately, an unsecured or incompatible driver's floor mat can trap the pedal wide open. Either condition can cause very high vehicle speeds and difficulty stopping, risking a crash.
records.solution: Have a GM or Toyota dealer perform the recall remedies free of charge: a reinforcement bar installed in the pedal assembly (or pedal replacement) for the sticky-pedal defect, plus the floor mat interference remedy. Verify completion via a NHTSA VIN recall lookup and never stack aftermarket floor mats.
symptoms: Accelerator pedal slow to spring back
Pedal feels rough, hard to press, or notchy
Pedal sticks partially depressed
Engine RPM stays high after releasing the pedal
Floor mat edge sits on or near the pedal
